statement: Kim has 7 cat cards and 5 dog cards. She makes pairs, and both cards in a pair must show the same animal. What is the largest number of pairs she can make?

choices.misconception: I only counted the pairs of dog cards.
I only counted the pairs of cat cards.
I put all 12 cards together and halved them, but a cat card and a dog card cannot make a pair.
I counted the cards, not the pairs.

hints: Make the cat pairs and the dog pairs separately.
Pairs only form inside each animal. An odd number of cards always leaves one card alone. Count the pairs for each animal, then add.
7 cat cards make 3 pairs with 1 card left over. 5 dog cards make 2 pairs with 1 card left over.

solutions.reliable: Cat cards: 7 = 2 + 2 + 2 + 1, so 3 pairs and 1 card left over. Dog cards: 5 = 2 + 2 + 1, so 2 pairs and 1 card left over. In all 3 + 2 = 5 pairs, with 2 cards that cannot be paired. The idea to keep: an odd group always leaves one out, so two odd groups leave two out.
solutions.elegant: 12 cards would make 6 pairs, but each odd group strands one card. Two cards are stranded, so the other 10 cards make 5 pairs. The idea to keep: count what is left over, then pair the rest.

whyOnTest: Odd and even: each odd group leaves one card without a partner, which is why halving all 12 cards gives too many pairs.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
